newsitem.title: SPAIN: Guatemala government, rebels sign accord in Madrid.
newsitem.headline: Guatemala government, rebels sign accord in Madrid.

text.p: The Guatemalan government signed an accord on Thursday with leftist rebels to reintegrate them into society and clear the way for a formal peace treaty ending Latin America's longest civil war.
The accord, signed in Madrid, was the last of three which precede a final peace agreement to be sealed on December 29 in Guatemala City.

"The interest of Guatemala demands first of all that the rebels are offered the means to join productive life under conditions of dignity," said Gustavo Porras, the Guatemalan government envoy who signed the agreement.
The series of accords put an end to 36 years of hostilies that have claimed more than 100,000 lives, mainly civilians. Another 40,000 have disappeared.
The agreement signed on Thursday outlines social, political and economic mechanisms to reintegrate guerrillas into a legal framework of civilian and political life.

"We are prepared to continue fighting, using legal means, to contribute to the country's development," said Pablo Monsanto, who signed on behalf of rebel forces of the Guatemalan National Revolutionary Unit (UNRG). To this end, the rebels will form a political party, he told reporters after the signing.

Under the terms of a ceasefire signed in Oslo on December 4, the UNRG agreed to be disarmed and concentrated in eight locations in Guatemala, where they will remain until they return to civilian life.
Monsanto said the rebel force numbers about 3,000 with another 1,500 supporters.
Porras gave further details on a timetable for implementing the accords at a news conference after the signing.
After the formal peace treaty is signed, the United Nations will set a ceasefire date from which the rebels will have 60 days to surrender their arms.
At the end of the 60 days, the government will have one year to integrate the rebels into civilian and political life.
President Alvaro Arzu's government has guaranteed the rebels employment opportunities, housing, sanitation, education and a national reconciliation under which war crimes will be forgiven.
The government and rebels also concluded a pact on constitutional and electoral reform in Stockholm on December 7. The peace agreements took five years to negotiate.
Spain has been supporting the Guatemalan peace process since 1994 along with Norway, Colombia, the United States, Mexico and Venezuela.
Spanish Foregin Minister Abel Matutes witnessed the accord on Thursday.
"Our commitment to the peace in Guatemala does not end with the signing of the accords because we are aware of the importance of changes which remain to be made," Matutes said.
